summary: Redwood Optimize walkthrough focusing on quantization profiles (INT8 vs FP8). Discussed quality vs latency tradeoffs, recommended profiling steps (pilot runs with sample prompts), and next steps: run benchmarks, share security docs, and scope Dedicated pilot. Customer concerned about latency for 99th percentile and data residency/KMS for PHI.
transcript:
00:00 Alex Chen: Hey everyone, thanks for joining, we wanted to go through the Optimize quantization profiles, specifically INT8 and FP8 and how those trade off quality vs latency. Quickly do intros?
00:08 Jordan Lee: Jordan here, CTO at NexaHealth, we've got Maria, Samir, and Lina on the call. We're mostly focused on clinical summarization workloads and some triage routing that needs tight p99 latency.
00:20 Alex Chen: Great, Alex from Redwood, AE, and Priya will lead the Optimize demo.
00:25 Priya Patel: Hi all, thanks. I'll share my screen, bear with me while the dashboard loads. (screen share chime) Can you see the Optimize console?
00:35 Maria Gomez: Yep, seeing it. A quick note — our data is PHI so we need private deployment or VPC and KMS integration.
00:42 Diego Ruiz: Totally, we can support Private or Dedicated with customer KMS, and we keep audit logs per request. We'll link the SOC2 and KMS docs after.
00:51 Samir Patel: Curious on quant profiles — we've heard INT8 gives big cost wins but worried about hallucination or slight quality drops on clinical text.
01:02 Priya Patel: That's exactly what this walkthrough is for. We'll show a couple of model variants: full FP16 baseline, FP8 profile (mixed FP8 where supported), and INT8 quantized runs. We'll cover latency (avg/ p95/p99), token throughput, and a simple quality metric — ROUGE-L on a labeled subset — plus sample outputs.
01:30 Priya Patel: First slide: overview. INT8 typically reduces memory and increases throughput but can degrade some quality depending on ops and layer sensitivity. FP8 (where supported) is a middle ground — often similar quality to FP16 but with some latency gains.
01:48 Jordan Lee: Do you have a prescriptive way to pick which layers to quantize? Our models are a custom T5 variant.
01:56 Priya Patel: Yes, our Optimize tool can generate quant profiles. It runs layer-sensitivity analysis across a small prompt corpus and outputs suggested per-layer quantization (e.g., keep first N layers FP16, quantize attention QKV to INT8 or FP8). We'll demo a sample profile we generated for a 3B T5-style model.
02:18 Priya Patel: Okay switching to the console. Here's the profiling job we ran for NexaHealth sample prompts — note the timeline at top, 15-minute run producing per-layer sensitivity charts.
02:30 Maria Gomez: The chart labels are a little garbled in the transcript earlier, sometimes it shows "KV cash" instead of KV cache in the automated captions, we've seen that.
02:38 Priya Patel: (laughs) yeah auto-captions get weird. So on the right you can see predicted latency curves if we apply INT8 globally versus hybrid FP8/FP16. See how the p95 jumps with INT8 for longer contexts?
02:55 Priya Patel: For our dataset the INT8 global quant reduced median token latency from 22ms to 12ms but p99 went from 110ms to 170ms on 2k context because of occasional kernel fallback and dequantization overheads.
03:10 Samir Patel: That's interesting — why would p99 get worse?
03:13 Priya Patel: Two reasons: first, INT8 can lead to kernel paths that aren't as well-optimized on certain hardware for long sequences, causing occasional slow ops. Second, our runtime may hit dequantization hotspots for KV cache refresh or during dynamic batching, which shows up in tails. Hybrid profiles (FP8 or keeping attention keys/values in FP16) often avoid that tail.
03:34 Jordan Lee: So is FP8 safer for us? We run on A100s and want consistent p99 < 200ms for triage.
03:41 Diego Ruiz: FP8 is a good middle ground, often keeps quality close to FP16 while giving latency/cost wins. On A100 and H100 it tends to be stable — but we still advise profiling with your specific prompts.
03:50 Priya Patel: Right. Here's the quality chart: baseline FP16 ROUGE-L 0.78, FP8 0.76, INT8 0.72 on this sample. The drop for INT8 was mostly on medically dense passages where tokenization and numeric fidelity matter.
04:10 Maria Gomez: 0.72 is pretty big drop for us, we'd need to set thresholds. Can you do targeted quantization so numeric-heavy layers remain FP16?
04:18 Priya Patel: Absolutely, that's the point of quant profiles. The tool recommends per-layer settings and you can manually override to keep sensitive layers in FP16. For example, keep embedding and initial attention layers FP16, quantize middle feed-forward to INT8.
04:34 Priya Patel: Also recommend running a few end-to-end evals — e.g., exact match on diagnosis codes and numeric extraction accuracy — because ROUGE isn't the full story for clinical tasks.
04:45 Jordan Lee: Good call. On infrastructure — what about Dedicated vs Hosted? For PHI we need private network and audit logs.
04:52 Alex Chen: For PHI we usually suggest Redwood Private (VPC/on-prem) or Dedicated with strict network peering and KMS. Both support our quant profiles and Optimize tooling; the difference is who manages the compute. Dedicated is managed by Redwood but isolated to your tenancy; Private gives you full control.
05:12 Samir Patel: If we pick Dedicated, can we run these profilers ourselves or do you run them?
05:16 Priya Patel: You can run Optimize jobs via API or Console. For initial pilots we can run them with you and hand over the pipeline so your infra team can run them later. The profiler docker image and instructions are in the docs.
05:30 Jordan Lee: Any caveats with cold starts and KV cache when switching quant modes? We've seen instability when models switch between quantized and non-quantized variants.
05:39 Priya Patel: Switches should be done via controlled rollouts — Canary route to quantized variant, and we wire up automatic fallback to FP16 variant if latency or quality SLOs degrade. KV cache format differences are handled by our runtime but full compatibility depends on exact model serialization; Optimize flags take care of that.
05:58 Maria Gomez: Can you show an example sample output difference live?
06:02 Priya Patel: Yep. Running three generations on the same prompt: prompt about discharge summary compression.
06:08 [06:08] Priya Patel (screen): "FP16 baseline: ..." shows detailed and accurate numeric vitals.
06:15 [06:15] Priya Patel: "FP8 output: ..." Very close, one minor rounding difference.
06:22 [06:22] Priya Patel: "INT8 output: ..." Slightly altered phrasing and one missing lab value.
06:29 Maria Gomez: That missing lab value is a deal breaker for us if it happens frequently. How often did that occur in your probes?
06:35 Priya Patel: In our sensitivity sweep it showed up in ~8% of cases on this dataset. But if you pin numeric extraction checks as rules, we can treat those as hard checks and exclude certain layers from quantization or route those prompts to FP16.
06:50 Jordan Lee: So could we do hybrid runtime: route high-risk prompts to FP16, others to INT8?
06:55 Diego Ruiz: Yes — smart routing by policy. You can tag routes, create inference policies that route by prompt classifier, latency vs cost tradeoff, or by customer tier. That way you get cost savings while protecting sensitive outputs.
07:10 Samir Patel: How do you measure cost delta? We need to show execs.
07:14 Alex Chen: Optimize includes cost estimates — token unit costs, GPU-hours, and amortized op costs under each profile. For example, in this run INT8 reduced token cost by ~38% but after accounting for occasional higher p99-induced infra overhead, net savings were around 28% for this workload. FP8 savings were ~18-22% with negligible quality loss.
07:40 Maria Gomez: Do you support mixed precision across the batch? Like some requests FP16 others INT8 in same worker?
07:46 Priya Patel: Batching mixed-precision in the same worker is tricky. Typically we separate worker pools by profile to avoid kernel mismatch — e.g., a FP16 worker pool and an INT8 worker pool; the router directs requests accordingly. That prevents tail latency from mixed kernels.
08:02 Jordan Lee: Any notes on library or kernel support? We run on H100 and A100.
08:07 Priya Patel: H100 and latest A100 CUDA stacks have good FP8 support; INT8 kernel maturity varies. We'll provide a hardware-compatibility matrix in the doc bundle.
08:16 Maria Gomez: Great. Can you also show the Optimize API call snippet?
08:20 Priya Patel: Sure — here's an example API: POST /optimize/profiles with sample prompts and model_id, returns recommended profile JSON plus per-layer sensitivity scores. (snippet pasted to chat)
08:33 Priya Patel: Note: the profile JSON itself contains per-tensor recommended dtype, but we also export a runtime-friendly pack that the serving runtime consumes.
08:44 Jordan Lee: About the benchmark spreadsheet — can you include p50/p95/p99 columns plus quality thresholds and an estimated cost delta?
08:51 Alex Chen: Yes we'll send the spreadsheet. It includes a sample workbook with pivot tables and per-prompt diff snapshots.
08:59 Lina Park: On compliance, do you keep request-level logs? We need retention and redaction controls.
09:04 Diego Ruiz: We keep audit logs; you can configure retention and redaction. For PHI we recommend Private deployment so logs stay in your VPC and KMS-managed at rest. We'll attach the SOC2 and data flow diagrams.
09:20 Jordan Lee: What's a typical pilot timeline and scope?
09:24 Alex Chen: Pilot typically 4–6 weeks: week 0 onboarding & sample collection, week 1 profile runs, week 2 quality/latency sweeps, week 3 integration and canary, weeks 4–6 monitoring and adjustments. For Dedicated pilot we can compress some steps if you provide infra access.
09:40 Maria Gomez: Cost for pilot?
09:43 Alex Chen: We usually provide pilot credits plus usage-billed components; we'll include pricing for Dedicated reserved capacity scenarios in the package.
09:50 Jordan Lee: Any specific risks to call out?
09:53 Priya Patel: Main risk is relying solely on generic ROUGE; recommend domain-specific validators for numeric extraction. Also tail latency surprises with INT8 on certain long-context workloads. That's why we recommend hybrid and canary rollouts.
10:10 Priya Patel: Quick demo of rolling to a canary: you can set rollout policy, enable canary at 5% traffic to INT8 worker pool, monitor p99 and quality checks, auto rollback if thresholds exceeded.
10:24 Samir Patel: How are quality checks enforced? Webhooks?
10:28 Priya Patel: You can configure evaluation hooks, which call your validator; also we support built-in evals and alerting in Console.
10:35 Jordan Lee: Ok, good. That covers most of our concerns. One last question: what's the difference in disk/serving footprint?
10:42 Priya Patel: INT8 model artifact is roughly 2.5–3x smaller than FP16, FP8 somewhere between. That reduces memory pressure and allows higher batch sizes, hence more throughput. But again, resource utilization patterns vary by model and sequence length.
10:58 Alex Chen: We're nearly out of time — want to recap next steps.
11:02 Jordan Lee: Sure.
11:04 Alex Chen: Priya will run a customer-specific latency/quality sweep using the prompt sets Maria will share, and we'll send the benchmark spreadsheet and security docs. Alex will follow up with pricing and pilot T&Cs. We'll schedule a POC scoping session week of Apr 6.
11:22 Jordan Lee: Sounds good. Thanks everyone.
11:25 Priya Patel: Thanks, bye.
11:28 [END]
